faq.credit: Answers summarised from the r/cardistry Cardistry Hub guide by u/LogicRevolution and the community.

items.a: Any deck works. Start with cheap standard Bicycle decks, since cards wear out fast while you learn. Paper, poker-size cards are best; plastic and bridge-size cards make many moves harder. Aladdin 1001, Tally-Ho, Copag 310 and Aviator are other cheap decks that handle well.

items.q: My hands are too small. What can I do?
items.a: They aren't too small: plenty of well-known cardists have small hands. Practise more, try a different grip, or use fewer cards while you learn. A few moves are harder with smaller hands, but most are possible.

items.q: Do I have to learn all the basics?
items.a: No. Pick the moves you enjoy. The basics do make later moves easier, so they're worth learning if you plan to stick with it.

Whichever feels comfortable. Most tutorials hold the deck in the left hand for right-handed people, and left-handed people usually use the right. If a tutorial is the wrong way round, mirror the video (VLC can flip it).

Little and often beats long sessions. Practise over a bed so dropped cards don't scatter, go slowly and smoothly before speeding up, focus on a few moves at a time, keep a deck nearby, and take breaks.

items.q: I can't get a move. Any tips?
items.a: Keep practising and rewatch the tutorial by the move's original creator. Search r/cardistry for others who asked about it, or ask in the Cardistry Discord with a short video of where you're at. Often the answer really is just more practice.

items.q: My hand hurts when I practise.
items.a: A light strain from using new muscles is normal. Real pain isn't: stop for a while, and if it comes back, see a doctor.
It helps. Finger exercises work, or simply run a few easy moves until your hands feel loose.

items.q: How do I take care of my cards?
items.a: Practise with clean, dry hands, keep cards away from humidity and dirt, and try not to drop them.

items.q: How do I break in a new deck?
items.a: Riffle and faro shuffles, swing cuts, springs and LePaul spreads all loosen a deck. Do them in both directions so the cards stay flat.

items.q: My cards click, bend or clump up. How do I fix them?
items.a: Humidity and temperature changes warp cards. Press them under something heavy, keep them in a card clip, or faro half the deck face-up into the rest and box it tightly. Springs and spreads in the opposite direction help too. If a deck clumps or won't fan, leave it alone for a few days.

items.q: When should I switch to a new deck?
items.a: When it's grimy, clumps, or no longer springs back into shape. Everyone's limit is different.

items.q: Do I need a card clip?
items.a: No. A clip protects the box and keeps the cards straight, which helps a deck last longer, but it's optional.

items.q: I made a move. Has anyone done it before?
items.a: If it's simple or combines basic moves, probably. Create for fun first; worry about whether it's original once the idea has grown.

items.q: How do I learn a move that has no tutorial?
items.a: Slow down a performance video, or ask the creator. Please don't learn from pirated tutorials or unofficial copies of paid ones.

items.q: What's the etiquette around paid moves?
items.a: Many cardists earn a living from their moves, so buy paid tutorials from the creator, don't make tutorials of other people's moves without permission, and always credit the creator.

items.q: Where can I meet other cardists?
items.a: r/cardistry, Instagram and the Cardistry Discord are the busiest places. Look for local jams, and Cardistry-Con is held each year.
